newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba seen holding rates steady despite M3.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba seen holding rates steady despite M3.

text.p: A slowdown in German money supply growth, a key Bundesbank policy indicator, gives the central bank little reason to ease its main money market interest rate in the near future, economists said on Monday.
"This is a number (the Bundesbank) can afford to ignore," said Alison Cottrell, senior international economist at PaineWebber in London.
She and other economists said they expected the Bundesbank to leave its three key interest rates unchanged when it holds a regular meeting of its governing council on Thursday.

The bank said September M3 money supply grew at an annualised, seasonally adjusted rate of 8.4 percent, meeting market expectations and reversing an unexpected acceleration when the rate climbed to 8.7 percent in August.
Both slower private sector lending and livelier monetary capital formation, a process by which money is shifted from bank deposits into shares and bonds, helped slow monetary growth in September.

As the annualised six-month private sector lending rate to September slowed to 6.3 percent after 7.1 percent, the annualised six-month rate for monetary capital formation rose to 5.5 percent from 4.6 percent.
"Now M3 growth is being squeezed from both sides," the monetary capital formation side and the private sector lending side, PaineWebber's Cottrell added.
Trinkaus Capital Management said firmer capital formation resulted from growing investor willingness to re-enter the securities market as fears about Europe's currency union waned.
But the welcome slowdown will not prompt the central bank to adjust interest rates again in the near term, largely because another reduction is currently unnecessary.

"We have quite a sound economic recovery in Germany now and we don't expect the Bundesbank to cut the securities repurchase rate," Petra Koehler, economist at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt said. The repurchase, or repo rate, is currently three percent. Cottrell said the Bundesbank could afford to hold off on adjusting monetary policy since the current appreciation of currencies against the mark had the same effect as a rate cut.

Another reason the Bundesbank may want to stick with its wait-and-see policy is to better assess the implications of Bonn's decision to defer a tax cut planned for 1997 and ongoing industry talks on 1997 wage contracts and sick payments, analysts said.
As the M3 figures met market expectations, the bond market barely moved on the number.
"There was nothing in that number for the market," said Graham McDevitt, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
Looking ahead, economists said M3 growth would continue to slow in coming months, particularly as private sector lending is likely to remain weaker as the economic upswing remains moderate.
Few, however, expected M3 to hit the central bank's four to seven percent target corridor.
"I still think its is going to be difficult to reach the M3 corridor this year," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer.

But even this fact would not worry the Bundesbank, economists said, noting the bank had stuck to its policy of setting monetary targets despite missing its goals in the past more often that it hit them. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
